title: Guitar
intro: The guitar is a fretted string instrument: six strings over a neck divided by metal frets into semitones. This topic covers the instrument, how to tune and read it, the basic techniques, and above all guitar theory: how the music theory of the piano maps onto the fretboard.

items: Classical (nylon-string): wide flat neck, soft warm tone, played with the fingers. Classical, flamenco and bossa nova.
Steel-string acoustic: brighter and louder, narrower neck; folk, country, singer-songwriter music. Played with a pick or fingers.

Electric: solid or hollow body with magnetic pickups that turn string vibration into an electrical signal for an amplifier. Light strings and low action make bends and fast playing easy; the amplifier and effects shape the sound.
Bass guitar: four (or five) strings tuned an octave below the guitar's lowest four, E1 A1 D2 G2; it plays bass lines rather than chords.
Headstock with tuning machines (tuners) that tighten or loosen each string.
Nut: the slotted bar where the strings leave the headstock; it is 'fret 0'.
Neck and fingerboard (fretboard) with frets, metal strips that each raise a string by a semitone. Most guitars have 19 to 24 frets; inlaid dots mark frets 3, 5, 7, 9, 12 (double), 15, 17, 19, 21.
Body: on an acoustic, a hollow box with a sound hole whose top amplifies the strings; on an electric, mostly solid wood carrying pickups, volume and tone controls.
Bridge and saddle: anchor the strings to the body; the saddle is the other end of the vibrating length (the scale length, about 648 mm on a Fender and 628 mm on a Gibson).

blocks.text: A string's pitch is inversely proportional to its vibrating length. A fret placed so the remaining length is $2^{-1/12}$ of the previous one raises the pitch by one equal-tempered semitone. The 12th fret sits at exactly half the scale length (an octave), and each fret space is about 5.6% narrower than the one before, which is why frets get closer together up the neck. The fret positions are therefore built for equal temperament (see Temperaments (#/arts/music-theory/tuning/temperaments)).
